  1. Emerging tool with a demand that it has not yet met (global black markets + unstable national economies). More real-world value will be converted into cryptos, increasing the real-world value of each token.
  2. Mathematically deflationary - some cryptos have a hard cap on the total # of tokens, others have a fixed rate of issuance. This basically guarantees that in the long run, the real-world value per-token of cryptos that are not declining in use, will go up.
  3. Newer privacy-first tokens (Monero and ZCash, primarily) make it mathematically/cryptographically impossible for anyone other than the two involved parties in a transaction to know the details of that transaction. This has far-reaching implications for the practices of government taxation, asset seizure, law enforcement detective work, and consumer tracking. As this technology makes its way out of the cryptocurrencies where it is first applied and into other things, a whole lot of governmental & corporate surveillance & control mechanisms may become obsolete. This is exciting!
  4. Token of value is tied to knowledge of a secret, not physical possession of an object (e.g. dollar bills) and certainly not to a company's record of the # of points in your account ("electronic banking"). For some people, this feels like it would be much harder to be taken away from them (asset freeze) than a physical object (fiat dollar bills), and this is attractive.
  5. The responsibilities for cryptocurrencies' valuation and execution and availability is implicitly spread across all the users. When adoption is small, it's easier for one malicious actor to influence a large-enough part of the network to pump-and-dump. As adoption grows, the ability of any one person to commit acts to the general detriment of the overall community decreases. Just like with stocks, largely-unknown penny stocks are much more susceptible to "pump & dump" than the household names like Apple, Microsoft, Google, etc - there are too many "honest" (or at least self-interested) players & too much real-world value for a single malicious entity to make a large splash.

Our reliance on government issued tokens is actually quite recent, only 200 - 300 years*. And while trading with bits of paper has advantages over using (say) gold rounds, it also has a few huge security flaws:

  • It assumes that only the government is capable of printing those tokens. If someone else can print passably similar tokens then the holders of government tokens lose wealth

  • It assumes the government itself is trustworthy, and won't print tokens in order to enrich itself or it's favorites

  • It assumes that the government won't leverage their position as the sole controller of all currency to punish individuals for breaking it's rules.

In all of those categories almost all currencies fail to some extent or other. The latter security flaw is even embraced as a virtue by keynesians, ie. almost all politicians and civil servants.

So to sum up, history shows that we have this money shaped hole on our head, which we fill with whatever tokens are convenient. We have used many different methods to supply this need over the years. The current dominant technology is to have cheap tokens printed by a giant central corporation with a monopoly over a huge area, we then trust this corporation to act ethically.

Crypto-currenies offer an enormous advance over this "trust us" system of currency. It requires no trust at all and it's virtually impossible to corrupt or control. It seems to fill the money shaped hole in our head just as well as any other token made from paper or metal, but it does so with much less risk of forgers or inflation.

And that's why you should seriously consider putting at least some of your wealth into crypto.
